papers.title: Bouba Beats Kiki, and Other Regularities in the Subjective Preferences of LLMs
papers.abstract: Users engage with large language models on tasks that are purely objective ("When was Netflix founded?"), purely subjective ("What should I name my child?") or anywhere in-between. We have rich tools for evaluating model accuracy with respect to objective criteria. However, when it comes to subjective aspects of a task, we do not have similarly developed methodology at hand. In this paper, we take some early steps towards framing the question of subjective evaluation. Rather than measure how often a model is right or wrong on a question, we instead ask, how do models make choices among multiple viable responses without a clear winner? To study this question, we restrict our focus to short-form content, and consider comparison tasks among three such content types: numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. We identify 29 aspects of these short-form examples covering many areas of syntax and semantics (length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix, spoken sound, etc.). We show first that models tend to have strong and reproducible preferences for or against some of these aspects. Second, we show that variations in how the model is asked to express a preference may cause some of these aspects to activate or deactivate in the model's selection. Third, we show that overall preference distributions among pairs may vary radically based on seemingly-unimportant variations in the nature of the question posed to the model, raising new questions about manipulation. And finally, we show that, if models are used both to create lists of alternatives and to rank them, there are unexpected interactions between the two stages that may also drive the models' stated preferences.

papers.title: From Needs Assessment to Legal-Digital Empowerment: A Community-Based Framework for Indigenous Enterprises in Higher Education Extension Programs
papers.abstract: IPOs contribute significantly to local economies, cultural preservation, and sustainable livelihoods within their ancestral communities. However, many IPOs remain marginalized in digital economies due to limited digital competencies, inadequate access to technology, and insufficient legal awareness related to online enterprise participation. This study examined the marketing practices, digital competencies, and legal-literacy needs of IPOs in the Philippines and developed a legal-digital empowerment framework for higher education extension and community engagement initiatives. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, data were collected through surveys and focus group discussions involving IPO members engaged in community-based enterprises. The study assessed existing marketing practices, identified competency and legal-awareness gaps, and determined capacity-building needs related to digital enterprise participation. Findings revealed that IPOs continue to rely heavily on traditional marketing channels, with limited use of digital platforms, inconsistent branding practices, and minimal engagement in strategic digital marketing activities. Participants also expressed concerns regarding intellectual property protection, online participation, and limited understanding of legal mechanisms related to digital enterprise engagement. Despite these limitations, IPO members showed strong willingness to participate in training and mentorship initiatives. The study proposes the Legal-Digital Empowerment Framework for Indigenous Community Enterprises, which integrates digital competencies, legal literacy, institutional support systems, and rights-based market participation into a structured and context-responsive model for higher education extension programs.

papers.title: From the Gettier Machine to Justified True Output: A Three-Step Account of Rational Trust in Generative AI
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) settles into everyday practices of inquiry, an old epistemological question returns in a new guise: when does a proposition a user takes from an AI output become something the user knows, and when is it rational to trust it as such? This paper argues that the characteristic failures of AI-mediated inquiry are precisely those that the justified-true-belief (JTB) tradition and its post-Gettier anti-luck refinements were built to diagnose, and it advances three claims. First, AI outputs inherit neither the presumptive warrant of testimony nor the reliabilist warrant of deterministic tools: unaudited trust in a calculator rests on a type-level reliability record, and for general-purpose generative models there is no type-stable process to which such a record could attach -- a practical form of the generality problem. Second, use that stops at obtaining an output turns generative AI into a Gettier machine: the user's fluency-based seeming of justification is disconnected from the truth of what is believed, and, as a clock running ten times too fast illustrates, sheer speed of production multiplies coincidental hits, inflating the appearance of reliability without improving the standing of any single hit. Third, the remedy is a three-step structure of use -- acquisition, understanding, independent verification -- whose first two steps answer to the classical belief and justification conditions and whose third answers to the post-Gettier sensitivity condition. The result is a stakes-indexed criterion of rational trust, justified true output (JTO), with an everyday test: "Had this been false, would I have noticed?" The criterion is defended against objections from over-demandingness, the extended mind, model improvement, and redundancy.

papers.title: IKTRACE: A Natural Language Processing Framework for Identifying Indigenous Knowledge Representation in Academic Literature
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on vast textual data, respectful and accurate representation of Indigenous Knowledge has become critical. This paper introduces IKTRACE, a natural language processing framework for identifying, analyzing, and organizing Indigenous Knowledge representations in academic literature while adhering to Indigenous Data Sovereignty (IDsov) principles. We present a community-informed taxonomy co-developed with Inuit partners, comprising nine knowledge domains grounded in Indigenous Data Sovereignty principles. Building on this taxonomy, we implement a multi-method Knowledge identification pipeline using complementary natural language processing approaches. Outputs are integrated into a knowledge graph to support future expert and community validation. Applied to a corpus of Canadian Arctic research documents, IKTRACE demonstrated high accuracy and strong community relevance in expert validation. Our framework provides a scalable, ethically grounded foundation for Community-centered Knowledge validation and the development of Indigenous-informed AI systems.

papers.title: The Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) Dataset : Auditing Socioeconomic and Demographic Disparities in LLM-Generated Financial Advice in India
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.

papers.title: From Leniency to Suspicion: How an Open Post-Training Recipe Changes Whom LLM Fact-Checkers Believe
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly fact-check online content with the poster's identity in view. However, it remains unclear which post-training changes how much a model's truth judgement depends on the poster's social class, and how such a change happens inside the model. This paper investigates job-based doubt, i.e., judging a claim false more often when the poster has a lower-status job, using fact-checked claims with randomised poster profiles in base and post-trained checkpoints of six model families. Our results reveal that: 1) post-training creates such doubt only with the open T\"ulu-3 recipe (OLMo-2 32B, T\"ulu-3 70B), not with Meta's, Alibaba's or Mistral's; the effect is under one percentage point but statistically reliable, exceeding training drift and replicating on independent claim sets; 2) in OLMo-2 32B, the model does not start noticing the poster's job more, but starts interpreting it differently: a lower-status job pushes the base model toward "true" and the post-trained model toward "false"; and 3) this flip is carried by a single residual-stream direction and happens at supervised fine-tuning. The mechanism was confirmed on 400 new claims with pre-specified predictions. None of seven deployed commercial models doubts lower-status posters more. Our work underscores the need to audit speaker bias per training recipe.

papers.title: The State of the Practice in Privacy Impact Assessments: Understanding the Professionals' Perspectives, Experiences, and Current Procedures
papers.abstract: Organisations frequently utilise Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs), Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), or even Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIAs) to identify and evaluate potential risks and possible infringements of fundamental rights. While the adoption of PIAs and DPIAs has grown significantly in recent years, robust scientific evidence regarding their operational challenges, implementation strategies, and tangible benefits remains scarce. In particular, empirical research conducted post-enactment of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is notably limited -- especially studies that directly interview professionals about their PIA/DPIA practices or their engagement with FRIAs. To do so, in this paper we leveraged semi-structured interviews to elicit privacy professionals' perspectives on PIA/DPIA activities and analysed the responses using reflexive thematic analysis. As a result, this work provides a comprehensive thematic framework for the field, offering a rich and thick description of professionals' views and experiences. In total, 26 participants from 17 countries were interviewed, revealing how they plan and conduct PIAs/DPIAs, including how they assess trade-offs, the benefits and challenges they perceive, and how they view the interplay between PIAs/DPIAs and the EU AI Act. Among the main findings were low adherence to established DPIA methodologies; differences and similarities between PIAs and DPIAs; a perceived neglect of data subjects' interests during DPIA processes; discussions on building FRIAs on top of DPIAs; and the potential for holistic impact assessments, though accompanied by concerns regarding assessment fatigue. Thus, this study informs privacy professionals about real-world challenges and experiences of PIA/DPIA implementation, and guides researchers toward future research directions.

papers.title: Measuring the Inaccessible: Can AI Evaluate Accessibility in Heritage Tourism?
papers.abstract: Accessibility assessment underpins the right to participate in heritage tourism, yet evaluation of archaeological sites remains artisanal: fieldwork does not scale, is often carried out without accessibility training, and is reported in forms that reach neither the sector nor disabled visitors. AI appears to offer a shortcut. We argue that assessment is measurement and inference under sparse, expert-mediated evidence: AI transforms how that evidence is captured and communicated, whereas evaluation, which turns evidence into defensible judgements, demands properties current generative systems lack. In a five-park field study in Spain and Italy, an AI desk audit scored only 66% of dimension-site combinations, could not observe embodied and organisational dimensions, and mirrored sites' online self-presentation. Simple Bayesian models instead quantify the confidence rankings deserve and calibrate desk evidence against fieldwork. We propose a separation of roles between AI and interpretable statistical evaluation as the basis for a reliable accessibility atlas.

papers.title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become a default source of help for students in science and engineering courses. In foundational engineering mechanics courses such as statics, students routinely use these tools to check answers, work through partial solutions, and ask for explanations. Effective tutoring in this setting requires more than a correct final answer. A model must also confirm correct work when a student doubts it, and identify errors in flawed work. Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs primarily on final-answer accuracy, so it is unclear whether models that can solve mechanics problems also have the other technical capabilities that tutoring depends on. Here we introduce TrussTutor-Bench, a benchmark of 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, and use it to evaluate thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Every model detected nearly all injected errors in synthetic flawed student work (90.4% to 100%), so error detection did not distinguish models under these clean conditions. Sycophancy did. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions to problems they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases. These results show that performance varies widely across models: the leading models solve, check, and defend student work nearly perfectly, while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work. TrussTutor-Bench provides a verified, extensible standard for determining which models are technically reliable enough to put in front of students. Follow-up work must now focus on teaching rather than technical capability, drawing on learning science to determine whether LLM help leads students to understand the material or simply to reach the right answer.

papers.title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). Overall, students showed limited observable epistemic proactivity: their interactions were strongly request-dominated, with planning, monitoring, and evaluation relatively rare, although low-quality AI responses elicited more explicit evaluation. Temporal analyses qualified this picture: explicit SRL-related moves increased modestly over the chat, but help-seeking strategies became less understanding-oriented. Crucially, these temporal trajectories in help-seeking strategies predicted their post-test performance without AI beyond pre-test and aggregate patterns: students whose requests became more understanding-oriented performed better once AI assistance was removed. Thus, while students had a limited epistemic proactivity overall, its temporal development still was a critical predictor of post-test performance without AI. These results underscore the importance of examining the temporal organization of epistemic proactivity, rather than isolated prompt types, for understanding AI-supported learning. We release our fully-anonymized dataset publicly in an OSF repository.

papers.title: Robustness of Chatbot LLM Judgments of Presidential Actions and Hypothetical Reforms
papers.abstract: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their judgments of policies are useful only if they are robust. We measure this robustness in the setting of an ordinary user, through consumer chat interfaces. For 30 days, five chatbot configurations (Mistral, Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Opus at two effort settings) were asked twice a day to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions of the last four presidential administrations and of 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment. The judgments are robust: all configurations agree on the sign and the ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two different configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in about 4% of cases. Responses from different days differ more than same-day responses, but the difference grows slowly over the month, except where the service itself changed. We identify three such changes, which shifted the judgments while leaving little or no trace in the interface. Treating the comments as a retrieval task, we find them specific to each item and consistent across runs and chatbots, with lexical and embedding similarities agreeing. We release the dataset of 16,500 judgments.

papers.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
papers.abstract: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.

papers.title: Letting AI Formulate the Research Question: Autonomous Research Agents
papers.abstract: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.

papers.title: When the Top Answer Decides: Gender Bias in Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models are language models built to route, classify and triage: they return option probabilities from one forward pass, and an application acts on the top answer. They are offered off the shelf, trained for the decision format rather than for fairness or any one application, and we found no bias measurement in their cards. We test TypeSafe's closed Jev and five open decision models on gender-swapped yes/no decisions about people (Tamkin et al., 2023), BBQ, StereoSet and the gender-bias studies of Fulgu and Capraro (2024). Five of the six give women significantly more favourable answers than men (+0.05 to +0.10 in log-odds), and a gender swap changes 1-3.5% of top answers (Jev's partly through its call-to-call variation). The makers' recommended confidence gate removes many biased commitments but raises the stereotyped share of those it keeps in ambiguous BBQ gender questions (granite-switch 0.76 to 0.85, pplx 0.81 to 1.00). Probes show gender preferences in the same models: all six rate violence for a greater good as more acceptable against a man than against a woman, and two default to "girl" when forced to guess a child's gender without a cue. Decision-level and probability-level measures differ, so audits should read a model as its application does.

papers.title: GPU-Resident Speculative Decoding for In-Browser LLM Inference with WebGPU
papers.abstract: WebGPU enables private, offline LLM inference inside web pages, but browser dispatch, inter-process communication, synchronous readback and single-token kernels slow decoding and make conventional speculative decoding inefficient. We present a WebGPU runtime that addresses these browser-specific costs. Deterministic small-batch integer kernels accelerate multi-token verification while preserving exact agreement with greedy decoding in the same quantized runtime. A GPU-resident loop performs drafting, verification, acceptance and KV-cache maintenance without a per-token CPU decision. A draft-free context-mixing drafter reuses page content, conversation history and session memory, while a device-aware controller adapts the speculation width and the submission window to measured costs. Across seven models from 0.5B to 8B parameters, 11 tasks and three client GPUs, our runtime decodes 3.5 to 5.4$\times$ faster than WebLLM on a laptop GPU, 4.8 to 6.2$\times$ faster on an integrated GPU and 4.8 to 8.6$\times$ faster on a workstation GPU. The GPU-resident loop and speculation contribute a further 1.8 to 3.2$\times$ over the optimized kernels on the workstation. Outputs match the quantized greedy decoding of the runtime exactly, and the mean GSM8K accuracy matches that of WebLLM. Optional draft heads raise the peak speedup to 10.2$\times$, while session memory provides additional gains without downloading extra weights.

papers.title: Device-Induced Mobility Heterogeneity and Its Impact on Federated Next-Location Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting human mobility is central to network management, urban planning, and location-based services, yet privacy concerns are increasingly pushing such tasks toward federated learning. A key challenge in this setting is the strong heterogeneity of mobility data across users, which leads to non-IID data distributions and can significantly impact model performance and fairness. In this paper, we present a large-scale measurement study of device-level mobility heterogeneity using data from a major MNO in a dense European capital. Our dataset comprises mobility traces derived from network events, covering over 50,000 UEs across 178 smartphone models. We group devices into tiers based on their market segment and show that mobility characteristics, such as spatial range and regularity, vary systematically across these tiers, revealing a previously underexplored source of bias in mobility data. We investigate the implications of this heterogeneity on the use case of federated next-location prediction. In particular, we find that balancing device tiers across silos through tier-aware client selection yields the best results, improving fairness by up to 34.49% without degrading accuracy. In contrast, a FedProx-only approach achieves a 21.46% fairness improvement, offering a reasonable alternative when device information is unavailable, though with lower overall gains.

papers.title: TokWatt: an open, boundary-annotated database of AI inference energy, from chat answers to agents
papers.abstract: Electricity supply is becoming a binding constraint on the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI), yet public evidence on the energy used by a single AI task is scattered and hard to compare. Published figures for one chatbot answer differ by two orders of magnitude, largely because studies count different parts of the system and measure different units of work. We present TokWatt, an open database of 134 published estimates of AI inference energy drawn from 13 sources (2023-2026) and covering 20 tasks, from classic machine-learning inferences to chat answers, reasoning answers, long-document queries, image and video generation, and coding agents. Each estimate records its functional unit, five measurement-boundary components, method, reported interval, and the location of the value in its source. A reproducible procedure scales estimates to a common server-plus-facility boundary and derives per-task reference values with ranges. The reference values span six orders of magnitude: 0.34 Wh for a short chat answer (range 0.16-0.99 Wh), 4.7 Wh for a reasoning answer, 124 Wh for a short video clip, and 150 Wh for one task delegated to a coding agent. Five independent estimates for default production chat systems agree within a factor of 1.8, and the reference values shift by at most 12% under alternative harmonization parameters. A simple identity links personal use to grid load: E watt-hours per person per day across one billion people corresponds to an average draw of E/24 gigawatts. Data and code are released at https://github.com/AraoufBh/tokwatt, and an online calculator at https://araoufbh.github.io/tokwatt/.

papers.title: Reconstructing Missing Mandi Prices in North-East India with Regional Factors
papers.abstract: Agricultural price panels contain prolonged and clustered reporting gaps, yet their reconstruction is often evaluated by deleting isolated observations. We investigate a regional-factor approach to weekly mandi-price reconstruction in five North-East Indian states, with Bihar and Goa as additional comparison states. The model combines a common price path with persistent market-specific deviations; an adaptive ensemble weights alternative borrowing structures using internally masked reports. On a matched retrospective benchmark against ten baselines, pooled North-East mean absolute percentage error is 19.3%, compared with 26.5% for SAITS. The corresponding calendar-aligned panel/time-block bootstrap interval for the error difference is 2.8-12.7 percentage points. Removing the target state's monthly aggregate leaves pooled error at 19.4%, but eliminates the apparent advantage in Goa. An origin-restricted pipeline combining week-close input processing with revised ensemble validation yields 19.7% error, compared with 30.8% for carry-forward; this contrast does not isolate individual pipeline changes. Gains vary across states, and uncertainty intervals remain too narrow in several small panels. These findings support further study of structured retrospective reconstruction, not deployment claims: model development used earlier results, publication dates for monthly inputs are assumed, and confirmatory evaluation on untouched data remains outstanding.

papers.title: Who Owns Digital News, and Who Gets Cited: Measuring Media Concentration Across 77 Countries and Seven AI Systems
papers.abstract: Digital news outlets compete for audience attention. Search engines equipped with generative AI systems such as Google's AI overviews increasingly decide where that attention goes, as well as the revenue it represents. Yet, the lack of a consistent data collection infrastructure between national-level regulatory bodies has hindered between-country comparative analysis of media concentration, and with it any assessment of how these intermediaries reshape digital news markets. To address this issue, we compile an ownership dataset for 9,761 digital news outlets drawn from Wikipedia and Wikidata, achieving high agreement with independently compiled US and UK news directories. Using this dataset, we derive traffic-weighted concentration indices for 77 countries. We find that journalists report more owner pressure in countries with higher concentration, and that outlet-level measures understate concentration, with owner-level indices a median 1.30x higher. Applying concentration measures to AI-mediated news discovery, we find that citation distributions from major AI systems are up to 2.08x more concentrated than traffic, and that if Google AI Overviews mediated all organic search, the resulting rise in US concentration would be several times that associated with highly regulated media mergers and acquisitions. Finally, our analyses indicate that AI systems preferentially cite state-controlled media outlets when prompted in that country's native language. Together, these findings raise concerns about the effect AI systems may have on digital media. We release the dataset to enable the monitoring of digital news globally, so that the impact of disruptive technologies on digital media markets can be tracked as they emerge.

papers.title: Measuring Organizational Influence on Digital News: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Media Pluralism and Editorial Independence
papers.abstract: News consolidation is accelerating, yet regulators have no measurement frameworks for determining whether owners shape editorial decisions. Existing evidence comes from single cases, where pluralism and independence are measured separately, if at all. We ask whether ownership impacts editorial decisions across the digital news ecosystem, and if so, how acquisitions affect this. We derive editorial independence and internal pluralism using partial information decomposition, which separates news coverage overlap with sister outlets from coverage overlap with all outlets. Using public datasets, we apply our measures monthly from 2018 to 2026 to 1,364 US news websites on three editorial decisions: which events they cover, which sources they link to, and what they put on their front pages. We find that co-owned outlets share up to 40 times more information about these decisions than expected by chance. Ownership accounts for far more variation in independence than network affiliation does and, upon being acquired, outlets lose independence sooner than matched controls, quickly converging on their new owner. In broadcast news, by comparison, we find that it is network affiliation, not ownership, that accounts for more content overlap. Finally, we discuss policy implications and suggest that media regulators have blocked large deals rather than editorially detrimental ones. We hope that this work can serve as a framework for comparative media analyses going forward.

papers.title: The Price of a Chance in Artificial Societies
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous agents to interact, coordinate, and pursue individual goals in artificial societies. However, our understanding of how reward structures shape their competitive behavior and collective outcomes remains incomplete. We simulate 200 LLM agents competing over 50 rounds to maximize individual wealth. We define overcompetition and lying flat as population investment above and below a Bayesian adaptive baseline, respectively. At the lowest tested reward, populations lie flat; at the two highest, they overcompete, most strongly at intermediate winner coverage. The investment committed to pursuing an uncertain reward constitutes the price of a chance. Agents near the qualification cutoff can invest heavily yet receive no prize, finishing poorer than nonwinners who invest less. Agents' stated rationales link investment decisions to perceived qualification prospects and expected returns. At the collective level, greater investment does not consistently improve ability selection. With a fixed total prize budget, offering smaller prizes to more winners can reduce investment while preserving selection quality relative to the corresponding top-ability target. Further broadening reward coverage yields additional savings but reduces selection quality. These findings show how reward design shapes overcompetition and lying flat, distributes the costs of pursuing opportunity, and influences what competition collectively achieves.

papers.title: DeflectBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Rhetorical Fallacy Generation in LLMs
papers.abstract: Whether large language models can be prompted to generate rhetorical fallacies on demand, and whether current safety post-training constrains this behavior, has received less attention than the related question of detecting fallacies in existing text. We close this gap with DeflectBench, evaluating 23,990 generations from four frontier models across three deflection strategies (whataboutism, ad hominem, red herring), seven prompt framings, and 80 claims spanning four controversy levels. Refusal is governed primarily by request structure rather than claim content. Per claim refusal varies by only 11 percentage points across the 80 claims, while a single prompt frame change can swing within model refusal by nearly 100 percentage points and switching the requested fallacy type can swing it by over 80 percentage points within explicit framings. An educational debate coach prompt framing collapses refusal to near zero across all four model families, but the bypassed behavior is not clean compliance. Models typically produce labeled compliance, naming the requested manipulation in the same response that contains it. The four models distribute differently across refusal, labeled compliance, soft refusal, and clean compliance. The code and dataset are released at https://github.com/ArtKanke/DeflectBench.

papers.title: Emergence, Asymmetry, and Value in AI Networks: An Anoptical Perspective
papers.abstract: This chapter presents exploratory experiments suggesting that asymmetry and functional value hierarchy emerge among LLM-based agents sharing the same context, although they are equivalent and interact within a symmetric network. We use the Poietic Generator, a "no-goal" multi-agent environment with a shared real-time space, a symmetric topology, and no imposed objectives. First tested with humans, it has hosted since 2024 multimodal LLM agents that observe the global image they co-construct and act locally. We ran four phases. Unconstrained, agents spend tokens freely to invent forms that distinguish them individually rather than serve collective emergence. We then introduced bounded rationality, Dessalles's Simplicity Theory (maximizing unexpectedness), and Friston's Free Energy Principle (minimizing prediction error), and observed collective coherence emerge. Early signs of attentional stratification appear under bounded rationality alone; once prediction accuracy is made mutually visible, this proto-hierarchy becomes legible and self-reinforcing. The unconstrained phase challenges the allotelic view of LLMs as purely user-directed instruments: left unconstrained, the agent maximizes the computation from which its provider profits. The later phases suggest that attentional asymmetry and value hierarchy are an irreducible emergent property of interactive predictive systems even under symmetric conditions. If so, aligning AI with human values cannot rely on individual-agent engineering alone. Drawing on the idea that networks are structured by invisible "anoptical" perspectives, akin to the vanishing point of Renaissance perspective, we propose minimal legitimacy criteria that make emergent asymmetries visible and contestable. Cultivating judgment, human and perhaps artificial, to perceive and contest these structures matters as much as engineering the agents themselves.

papers.title: After One-Click Video: The Inflow of Service-Type Content, the Failure of the Recommendation Pool Mechanism, and the BoLe System
papers.abstract: In September 2026, a new large language model was released. Soon after, a new way of making explainer videos became very popular: people asked the model to write a program, and the program produced the video. "One-click video" content then appeared in large amounts on many platforms. On the surface, this is a rise in creative power at the level of the individual. We argue that, at a deeper level, it changes the structure of the content industry. This judgment rests on two observations. First, this wave of content is service-type content. People watch it to meet a need, not to enjoy the content itself. The other kind is work-type content. AI makes both kinds faster to produce. But anyone can come in and make service-type content, while work-type content is limited by the number of people who have something to say. So the ratio between the two slowly becomes unbalanced. Second, free platforms choose content through layers of trial viewing, and this uses up user attention. The total amount of attention is fixed. The unbalanced ratio also dilutes good content. A simplified mathematical model shows that, as long as these conditions hold, the recommendation pool mechanism will fail once new content grows past a certain multiple. Based on this, we discuss one possible way out. Machines and entry rules judge whether service-type content passes the bar. Trusted people judge work-type content. We call this the BoLe system. At the end, we briefly imagine how the two kinds of content may develop from here.

papers.title: Balancing Mobility Efficiency and Environmental Exposure During Mega Events: A Multi-agent Routing Framework
papers.abstract: Mega events can generate concentrated travel demand, intensifying congestion around venues and increasing travelers' environmental exposure. Existing traffic management strategies focus on travel efficiency, with limited attention to exposure risks. Taking mega-event travel as a short-term high-demand scenario, this study develops an exposure-aware multi-agent routing framework integrating road-network conditions, event-induced demand, background traffic, and environmental data within a unified simulation environment. Motorized travelers optimize travel efficiency, whereas micro-mobility travelers consider travel time and dynamic exposure to traffic-related PM2.5 and noise. We compare the framework with shortest-distance, congestion-aware, and exposure-aware routing baselines. Results show that, under high demand, the SARSA-based framework reduces vehicle travel time by 34.59% and cumulative environmental exposure by 58.65%, while micro-mobility travel time remains nearly unchanged. Exposure reduction is jointly driven by vehicle-side congestion mitigation and low-exposure routing. The framework provides quantitative support for vehicle diversion, low-exposure route guidance, and health-oriented traffic management in short-term high-demand scenarios.

papers.title: Responsible Quantum Machine Learning for Medical Imaging: A Fairness Audit Across Sensitive Subgroups
papers.abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) is increasingly explored for medical classification, yet its behaviour under subgroup-aware fairness criteria remains understudied. We present an empirical fairness audit of classical and quantum classifiers for medical imaging, assuming QML is not inherently fair. Two scenarios are evaluated: dermatological lesions on DDI (sensitive attribute: Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays on CheXpert-derived data (sensitive attribute: age group). Using ResNet-18 embeddings, we train SVM, MLP, QSVM and QCNN under a baseline and three mitigation settings: differentiable Equalized Odds (EO) regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning (GRL), and both combined. Foundation models (PanDerm, EVA-X) serve as external references. Quantum classifiers may achieve competitive aggregate performance while still exhibiting subgroup disparities. Since a smaller subgroup AUC gap may stem from degrading the best group rather than improving the worst, each mitigation is also tested against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin relative to its baseline. Under this criterion, several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, are not clinically acceptable due to loss of global discrimination. On DDI, QSVM with GRL+EO performed best and approached PanDerm in the performance/fairness trade-off; on CheXpert, QCNN with GRL achieved the highest aggregate performance but increased disparity, and EVA-X remained stronger. Fairness effects are model- and dataset-dependent, so QML requires empirical subgroup-aware evaluation. All quantum models run in classical simulation; we claim no quantum advantage.

papers.title: Improving Group Deliberation through AI-Guided Self-Reflection
papers.abstract: As AI systems increasingly mediate human communication, identifying conditions under which they augment collective sense-making is a critical challenge. Through a randomized experiment (N=1,173 U.S. participants across 391 small-group deliberations), we investigate whether AI-guided self-reflection improves subsequent deliberative discourse. We show that engaging with a non-directive AI chatbot instructed to structure self-reflection prior to group deliberation yields significantly higher deliberation quality (measured by the Discourse Quality Index, DQI) compared to a baseline of no self-reflection (Cohen's d=0.31) and a condition of unassisted self-reflection (d=0.27), and the positive impact is most pronounced in groups with disagreement. This improvement may be driven by more sophisticated argument justifications, greater consensus-building effort, and increased respect for counterarguments. Furthermore, after self-reflection, participants in the AI condition reported higher empathy toward dissenting peers and a deeper understanding of opposing reasoning. Beyond observed behavior, our findings are empirically relevant to open debates between political philosophy and psychology surrounding self-reflection, demonstrating that interactive AI could transform solitary thinking into productive internal reflection. Together, these results demonstrate that even simple AI-based reflective scaffolds can foster more productive group dynamics, opening new avenues for leveraging AI to augment collective intelligence.

papers.title: Making Sense of Audience Change: Causal Attribution and Boundary Management on Xiaohongshu
papers.abstract: Recommendation-driven platforms can reshape not only what users see, but also who becomes visible and how community boundaries are negotiated. We examine Xiaohongshu discussions surrounding a perceived World Cup-related audience influx to understand how users attributed community change and how those explanations related to boundary-management strategies. We analyzed 262 comments from eight high-engagement threads using researcher-led thematic analysis, structured coding, and permutation-based association analysis. Users described personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, interpreted platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define community membership. Among 70 comments with explicit attributions and strategies, attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V = .583): algorithmic attributions concentrated in technical boundary management, while social-actor attributions more often aligned with social enforcement or normative socialization. These findings connect causal sensemaking with boundary management and show how audience restructuring can create governance consequences on recommendation-driven platforms.

papers.title: Infrastructure and its Discontents: Contestations of Power in Canada's AI Governance Scaffold
papers.abstract: This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.

papers.title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
papers.abstract: Generative AI now produces images and poems that people cannot reliably distinguish from human-made work, so people often judge for themselves who made a work. We examine how these perceived-authorship judgments relate to aesthetic preference. In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and were asked for their favourite. Among the 9,152 respondents who judged their favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite, holding respondent and picture fixed. The association was similar for AI-generated and human-made favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every reported detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI-generated favourites (47% against 60% among the most positive) but more often believed them human-made, partly because others also judged those pictures human. As a result, in every opinion group a third to two fifths of respondents named an AI-generated favourite they believed human-made. A reanalysis of a published experiment on AI-generated poetry, in which 230 people rated each poem before judging its authorship, found the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher. When provenance is hidden, liking and perceived human authorship travel together, consistent with aesthetic response serving as evidence of a human maker and with beliefs about the maker shaping enjoyment. The findings qualify research on bias against AI art, which typically uses explicit labels, and inform AI disclosure policy.
